# Fexofenadine hERG liability at therapeutic exposure

**No.** hERG liability is not a meaningful concern for fexofenadine at therapeutic exposure. This is well established from clinical and electrophysiology data, not just from the model.

## The experimental and clinical evidence

- **Origin.** Fexofenadine is the carboxylic acid metabolite of terfenadine. Terfenadine was withdrawn because of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes when its metabolism was inhibited, for example by ketoconazole or erythromycin.
- **Patch-clamp potency.**
  - Terfenadine blocks hERG potently, with an IC50 in the tens to low hundreds of nM.
  - Fexofenadine is roughly 2–3 orders of magnitude weaker. Reported IC50s are in the ~20–65 µM range, and some studies saw little block at 30 µM.
  - The carboxylate is the key difference. The zwitterion lowers lipophilicity and disrupts the binding mode in the channel cavity (Y652/F656). This is a classic example of adding an acid to remove hERG activity.
- **Exposure margin.**
  - At 180 mg, Cmax is about 0.5 µg/mL, which is roughly 1 µM.
  - Protein binding is 60–70%, so free Cmax is about 0.3–0.4 µM.
  - That gives a free Cmax to IC50 margin of about 50–100× or more, well above the usual ~30× comfort threshold.
- **Clinical ECG data.** Studies at doses well above the label (up to ~800 mg single doses and multi-day high-dose regimens) showed no clinically relevant QTc prolongation. Co-administration with ketoconazole or erythromycin raised exposure but did not prolong QTc.

## How to read the ToxPred output

- **What it says.** It predicts `non_blocker`, with P(blocker) of 0.25 against a threshold of 0.41. That agrees with the known biology.
- **Why it adds little here.**
  - It is a qualitative classifier. It gives no IC50, so it cannot address the question of exposure at therapeutic doses; only a potency-versus-free-Cmax comparison can.
  - The applicability check is only an element-composition rule. It says nothing about whether the structure falls within the model's domain.
  - Fexofenadine is a marketed drug and may well be in the training data. That would make this more of a recall than a true prediction.
- **Structural limitation.** The model probably cannot capture the terfenadine-to-fexofenadine change reliably. The two differ only by CH3 versus COOH. I wouldn't lean on it for matched-pair calls like this in your own series without patch-clamp confirmation.

## Side note on the PPARγ flag

The NR-PPAR-gamma prediction is active (0.87 against a 0.42 threshold). This is most likely driven by the lipophilic gem-dimethyl aryl-acetic acid motif, which is somewhat fibrate-like. There is no clinical PPARγ signal for fexofenadine, so I'd treat it as a structural false positive. If you see the same flag on analogs, though, it would be worth a counter-screen.

## Takeaway

Fexofenadine's hERG safety rests on a large potency margin and clean clinical QT data. The ToxPred result agrees but contributes little independent evidence. If you're using fexofenadine as a reference compound for a series, measured patch-clamp IC50s alongside projected free Cmax are the right comparison.
